Understanding YOLOv2 fish tracking

Paper explanation · October 28, 2026

Zebrafish tracking using YOLOv2 and Kalman filter, Barreiros et al., Scientific Reports (2021).

The central idea

Detect each fish’s head, then use motion to connect those detections across frames. This separates “where are the fish?” from “which fish moved where?” Source: paper.

How it works

  1. Learn what a head looks like. Researchers mark heads in training images and train YOLOv2, an object-detection neural network.
  2. Find heads in each frame. Overlapping image sections preserve detail; duplicate detections are removed.
  3. Predict movement. A Kalman filter estimates each fish’s next position and orientation.
  4. Match predictions to observations. A matching algorithm assigns detections to tracks; a later step reconnects interrupted paths.

Source: methods.

How to interpret the results

In feeding footage, detection precision was 99.87%, the miss ratio was 3.37%, and correct identity recovery after occlusion was about 83%. High precision means few false detections—not that every fish was found. Their tracking-rate metric excludes identity swaps. They used backlighting, reflection-reducing glass treatment, and 30-fps recordings. Source: methods and results.

What this means for Fish Cluster

The following is our engineering assessment. These proposals have not been implemented or validated in the app.

A learned detector would change the detection stage substantially. Our current approach asks which pixels differ from the tank background. A trained detector would instead look for visual patterns learned from labeled examples. We would need representative training images and independent testing.

Head position and body center are different measurements. If we adopted head detection, we should explicitly define what “fish position” means in distance calculations and exports. Mixing the two could change results.

Better tracking cannot guarantee better detection. Imagine two fish crossing: motion can suggest which way each continued, but that remains an estimate when the image does not distinguish them. Our review interface should preserve that uncertainty.

For isolated photos, the detector is the relevant part. Motion prediction requires a sequence. Evaluation should focus on the intended rectangular-tank setup; the five-fish round-tank example remains an optional stress test.

Recommended experiment

Investigate this architecture if detection remains unreliable on the actual tank setup. First test a head detector on a small labeled collection of representative frames, keeping evaluation images separate from training images. Compare missed fish, false detections, and position error with our current detector.

This would establish whether the additional model-training and browser-integration effort is justified before committing to a larger implementation.
